newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Croatia opposes renewing U.N. force in E. Slavonia.
newsitem.headline: Croatia opposes renewing U.N. force in E. Slavonia.

text.p: Croatian Deputy Prime Minister Mate Granic on Tuesday opposed any renewal of a U.N. operation in Eastern Slavonia designed to return the formerly Serb-controlled region to Zagreb's control.

"Any additional extension of the UNTAES (U.N. Transitional Administration for Eastern Slavonia) mandate in Croatia can only encourage delays in its implementation," he said in a speech to the General Assembly.
It would also place at risk the most critical aspect of the mandate -- the return of 80,000 non-Serb refugees and displaced people to the region -- he added.

The current one-year mandate of the 5,000-strong U.N. operation, headed by U.S. diplomat Jacques Klein, expires Jan. 5, 1997. But an accord signed last November between Croatia and local Serb authorities provides for an extension of up to another 12 months, if requested by one of the parties.

Granic, who is also Croatia's foreign minister, said continued lack of progress could induce both internal and external instability. "And this is a matter which my government should seek to avoid at all cost. For this reason, the clear stance of my government is that the pace of peaceful reintegration of the Danubian region under the present UNTAES mandate should be completed on schedule."

Granic said UNTAES "just may become the most successful peacekeeping operation in recent history, and perhaps rightfully so given our own and international frustrations with unsuccessful operations in the region so far."

He also said that, with the signing of a normalisation agreement between Croatia and Yugoslavia, comprised of Serbia and Montenegro, a small U.N. observer mission on the Prevlaka peninsula "shall also become obsolete in the predictable future." Most of the peninsula south of the city of Dubrovnik is controlled by Croatia, but it borders Montenegro and the main deep-water port for its navy.
The current mandate of the 28-member U.N. Mission of Observers in Prevlaka (UNMOP) expires on Jan. 15, 1997.

Granic said Croatia and Yugoslavia had agreed that the issue of Prevlaka should be resolved as a security matter according to the U.N. Charter and international standards for good neighbourly relations.

Rejecting any idea of an exchange of territory, he added: "Therefore, there shall be no further raising of the question of adjustments between Croatia and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia on the Prevlaka peninsula -- the five-century-old boundary between Croatia and Montenegro."
But he said there was a need to establish a security regime there through peaceful negotiations for mutual benefit.
